lesson.title: Flip and Scale: Deriving the Inverting Amplifier's Gain
lesson.summary: The inverting amplifier uses an input resistor and a feedback resistor around an op-amp, with the non-inverting input grounded, to produce an output that is a scaled and sign-flipped version of the input, with gain equal to -R2/R1.
lesson.body:
The inverting amplifier is one of the two foundational op-amp circuits, alongside the non-inverting amplifier of the next chapter, and nearly every more elaborate op-amp circuit, including the summing amplifier later in this unit, is built from the same reasoning used here. Its topology is simple: an input resistor R1 connects the input voltage Vin to the inverting input (V-) of the op-amp, a feedback resistor R2 connects the output back to that same V- node, and the non-inverting input (V+) is tied directly to ground.

Because V+ = 0 volts (real ground) and negative feedback is present through R2, the virtual ground condition from the previous chapter applies: V- also sits at 0 volts. This immediately gives the current flowing from the source through R1 into the V- node: by Ohm's law, I1 = (Vin minus V-) / R1 = (Vin minus 0) / R1 = Vin / R1.

Now apply the infinite input impedance assumption from the ideal op-amp model: none of this current can flow into the op-amp's V- terminal, since ideally zero current enters there. By Kirchhoff's current law, the only place this current can go is out through the feedback resistor R2 toward the output. Writing the current through R2 using the same node, from V- toward Vout, gives I2 = (V- minus Vout) / R2 = (0 minus Vout) / R2 = negative Vout / R2. Setting I1 equal to I2 (the same current, one path in, one path out): Vin / R1 = negative Vout / R2, which rearranges to Vout = negative (R2 / R1) times Vin. The closed-loop voltage gain of the inverting amplifier is therefore Av = negative R2 / R1, with the negative sign indicating that the output is inverted, 180 degrees out of phase with the input, exactly why the circuit carries the name it does.

As a concrete example, let R1 = 1 kilohm and R2 = 10 kilohms, with an input voltage Vin = 0.5 V. The gain is Av = negative 10 kilohms / 1 kilohm = negative 10, so Vout = negative 10 times 0.5 V = negative 5 V. We can verify this independently with the current method: I1 = Vin / R1 = 0.5 V / 1000 ohms = 0.0005 A, or 0.5 mA. This current has nowhere to go but through R2, producing a voltage drop of I times R2 = 0.0005 A times 10,000 ohms = 5 V across R2. Since that drop occurs from the 0 volt virtual ground node down to the output, Vout = 0 V minus 5 V = negative 5 V, matching the gain formula exactly.

One limitation worth noting: because the source driving Vin sees R1 connecting it to a virtual ground, the effective input impedance of this whole stage, as seen by the source, is simply R1, not the op-amp's own near-infinite input impedance. For sources that cannot tolerate a low-impedance load, this is a real drawback, and it is precisely the motivation for the non-inverting amplifier topology covered next, which lets the source drive the op-amp's naturally high impedance input directly.
